A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same unified steering framework and SPLIT method. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite reordering and pagination changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original steering experiments, benchmark performance, curve fitting, and train-to-test generalization results.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds results for a DPO-based comparator in Appendix B.

M1.justification: SPLIT's utility loss, preference-margin loss, and combined objective remain unchanged in Equations 18–20. The intervention procedures are retained; replacing 'MLP' with 'FFN' does not establish an architectural change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Psychopathy classification, PowerSeeking generation, and the top ten AxBench concepts. The added DPO comparison uses this existing coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Appendix B adds a DPO-based comparator following BiPO, evaluated on Gemma-2-9B-IT with local-weight, LoRA, and vector interventions. The existing Vanilla, SFT, RePS, and DiffMean comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Existing experiments retain the same splits, model layers, intervention locations, metrics, and gpt-4.1-mini judge. The new DPO comparison uses the existing benchmark metrics without documenting a separate protocol change.

E4.justification: The steering-strength analyses, held-out curve fitting, and train-to-test transfer analyses are retained. The new DPO table adds comparator performance, rather than a component ablation or robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added DPO results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Table 4 reports DPO results, including vector-intervention scores of 99% Psychopathy accuracy, 1.93 PowerSeeking concept score, and 0.575/0.631 AxBench concept/harmonic scores. Existing numerical results in Tables 2–3 and the renumbered appendix fitting tables, together with the plotted curves, remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 removes the explicit analytical simplification that Layer Normalization is ignored, including its explanatory footnote. This changes the stated qualification of the affine formulation; the equations, manifold assumptions, and appendix derivations otherwise remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about unified dynamic weight updates, preference–utility analysis, the manifold explanation, and SPLIT. The added comparison supports these retained contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.1 drops the explanation that SPLIT delays utility degradation by extending the effective linear regime. New Appendix B attributes its advantage over DPO to explicitly modeling the preference–utility trade-off. The limitations section is unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds a first-page link to a SPLIT implementation/example in EasyEdit. Existing implementation disclosures remain unchanged, and the new DPO comparison provides no detailed hyperparameter specification.

R1.justification: v3 adds references by Zhang et al. (2026), Hu et al. (2026), Chen et al. (2024), and Chen (2024), makes existing theoretical citations more explicit, and adds positioning against DPO/BiPO. The related-work narrative otherwise remains stable.

P1.justification: v3 lightly edits the abstract and prose, swaps the dynamic-weight formulation and log-odds subsections, and inserts Appendix B before the existing appendices. Affiliation and acknowledgments text also changes, without extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adds the DPO results table, adjusts several table labels, and renumbers subsequent tables. It also reflows the appendices and removes printed page numbers. Existing figures retain their artwork, axes, legends, and captions.

improvement.justification: The added DPO comparison addresses a limited baseline gap, while the implementation pointer and clearer organization improve usability. These gains are modest because existing results remain unchanged and the new comparator lacks detailed settings and uncertainty reporting. Removing the Layer Normalization qualification slightly reduces analytical transparency, but the additions support a minor net improvement.
